His latest collection, The Bootleg Sounds of Marshall Crenshaw: 1984-1987 , offers a peek into his process. Linus + Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy :: The Outsider: The Music of Jules Decorte Posted on November 12, 2026 November 3, 2026 Three oddly-shaped pieces come together in the most natural way in this under-the-radar release from Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy. The disc reconfigures the work of blind Dutch songwriter Jules de Corte, an outsider artist who wrote and recorded over 3,000 songs during his lifetime. This is not what you’d call a natural fit. De Corte’s songs are quick and witty and cerebral, more like cabaret or art song than BPB’s mournful Americana. Yet the two artists share an unconventional spirituality; there’s real searching in De Corte’s cleverly put together tunes. Habibi Funk 035 :: Beirut City Pop Posted on November 12, 2026 November 9, 2026 In a departure from the usual template of old photos of the artists, the cover of Habibi Funk’s latest reissue features an illustration by Beirut-born, Paris-based artist Raphaelle Macaron. Poolside beach chairs sit empty on the patio of a luxurious apartment complex at dusk, separated by red, rocky terrain from the city skyline in the background. Cool purples, pinks and blues saturate the scene in a clear nod to the style of Hiroshi Nagai, whose work graces the covers of Light in the Attic’s Pacific Breeze City Pop compilations of funk, soul and AOR from 1980’s Japan. But while the references in the album’s title and cover art lovingly highlight the parallels with the City Pop era, the contents of the album highlight the perpendiculars. Pastoral electronics, kosmische, fractured psychedelia, bent frequencies. 34.1090° N, 118.2334° W Lex Walton :: Ultimate Love Forever Posted on November 11, 2026 November 11, 2026 Lex Walton makes swaggering, theatrical, large-scale rock – the spit and snarl of her vocals punk laced, the instrumental arrangements swelling to arena-rock proportions. Dan Boeckner, half of one of the last big emotive rock duos of the aughts and teens, produced Ultimate Love Forever , and it has, sonically at least, some of Wolf Parade’s unabashed romanticism. The content is lacerating, the mood nihilistic, but the music itself is all about the good time. It high-kicks and cake-walks and vibrates with theatrical music hall energies. Transmissions :: Adam Voith Posted on November 11, 2026 November 10, 2026 Our guest this week is author Adam Voith, whose new novel, RIYL , short for “Recommended If You Like,” is an at times thinly veiled memoir of the ’90s Christian punk and indie scene. With echoes of Get in the Van and Freaks and Geeks, RIYL threads that delicate needle of looking back at earnest teenage corn doggery with warts and all embarrassment, tempered by the type of affection that only time and distance allow all of us. It’s also frequently flat out hilarious. Hiroshi Yoshimura :: Quiet Forest Posted on November 11, 2026 November 11, 2026 With no deceleration in sight, the 2020s have thus far been the decade of Kankyō Ongaku pioneer Hiroshi Yoshimura. 1996’s Quiet Forest , the musician’s final offering, is another gem in a slew of reissues courtesy of tireless label Temporal Drift. The Hoh Rainforest is the setting here, as Yoshimura interprets the terrain with his singular approach: superimposed synth soundscapes that contagiously mirror the greenery and precipitation: fluttering new age soundscapes as opulent as they are evocative. Ronnie Self :: The Lost Sessions Posted on November 10, 2026 October 28, 2026 Best remembered for the unhinged rockabilly of “Bop-a-Lena” and Brenda Lee’s “I’m Sorry,” Ronnie Self spent much of his later career writing songs that went largely unheard. The Lost Sessions , a collection of seventeen recordings from that period, finds him somewhere between country, folk-rock, and the lonely hours of the night. A long-overdue glimpse of the songwriter behind the legend. Bill Nace / Mike Polizze Duo :: Live at Pageant: Soloveev Posted on November 10, 2026 November 2, 2026 Live at Pageant is an incendiary slab of sound, a conflagration of Mike Polizze’s eruptive, corrosive, psychedelic guitar and Bill Nace’s equally untethered taishigoto. The music happened at Philly’s Pageant Soloveev gallery in early summer of 2025; it only exists in recorded format because Polizze pulled out his phone just before the music starts. Josh Johnson :: Animative Posted on November 9, 2026 November 7, 2026 Josh Johnson plays the saxophone like an orchestra in this third solo album, Animative . That will surprise no one who’s seen his live shows, frenetic, ebullient displays of the power of live looping, as one sax riff echoes another and another. Nimble, pointillistic “Idiophone” which starts off the album, juggles reed and electronic sounds like a circus plate spinner, a cerebral abstraction one moment, a funk-syncopated fusion dream the next. Call Mr. Lloyd :: A Brief Richard Lloyd Appreciation Posted on November 9, 2026 November 9, 2026 A restless farewell to Richard Lloyd! The musical “alchemist”—a self-selected term—passed away on November 7. In tandem with Tom Verlaine in Television, Lloyd helped rewrite the rules when it came to the electric guitar in a rock setting. Lloyd was a player of boundless technical skill and unbridled imagination—a potent combination, to be sure. When Lloyd launched into a solo, every note was life or death, every moment a high-wire act of wildly impassioned delight. Here, a small sampling of the man’s six-string genius. Jon Hassell :: Music Is Invisible (Pentimento Volume Three) Posted on November 9, 2026 November 9, 2026 Music Is Invisible marks the third and final entry in Jon Hassell’s Pentimento trilogy. Arriving five years after the experimental trumpeter’s death, it’s not exactly a studio album, but it’s more than a live tape. As a record of a singular artist’s psychic terroir, strong, mutable style and idiosyncratic sonic palette, it’s a fittingly puzzling send-off. But rare elements of “straight Hassell” lurk in the mix, for those with the ears to see. Felt :: Be Still (The Beach Boys) Posted on November 6, 2026 November 2, 2026 Toward the tail end of their ten-album run in the eighties, English jangle pop outfit Felt had sights on 1968’s understated Beach Boys classic Friends for the band’s only known cover. This transformative take on Dennis Wilson’s soulful, momentary piano ballad “Be Still” sits comfortably next to Primal Scream’s Screamadelica -era cover of another Dennis gem in “Carry Me Home” (keyboardist Martin Duffy would play in both bands). A shimmering beauty reminiscent of every frosty, ethereal component of the brilliance of Felt.
